title: Secrets in code

story: When Nova's run for RH-1234 starts, the broker hands Nova's machine a capability: a long random string that means "whoever shows me this may push to the branch nova/RH-1234 and comment on RH-1234, and nothing else, until this run ends". Together with a run token for Claude, it is all the machine holds: no GitHub token and no key ever reach it.

Now imagine three small mistakes in the first version of the broker. It stores the capabilities in its database as they are, and a copy of that table is saved in a backup that thirty people can read. A debug line prints req.headers, so every capability also lands in the log system. And the check is written as presented === stored, which, as you will see, can give away a little of the answer with every wrong guess. None of these mistakes looks dangerous in a pull request.
hook.question: How do I make a token that nobody can guess, store it so that a leaked database is useless, check it without giving hints, and keep it out of every log?

p: A capability is only safe if nobody can guess it, so it must come from real randomness. Node's built-in node:crypto module has randomBytes, which asks the operating system for secure random bytes. 32 bytes are 256 bits: even trying a billion guesses a second, an attacker would need far longer than the age of the universe. As hex, the bytes become 64 characters that are safe in an HTTP header.

Math.random() is the wrong tool. It is built to be fast, not secret, and with enough of its outputs its next ones can be predicted. Use it for a random colour in a UI, never for anything that opens a door.

notes.text: All three come from Node itself; no package needed.
A hash function: the same text always gives the same 32 bytes, and the bytes cannot be turned back into the text.
32 secure random bytes, written as 64 hex characters.
The caller hands the capability to the machine once and keeps only the digest.
Hash what was presented, then compare the two digests. The next sections explain both steps.

read.h: Keep the hash, not the token
p: A hash such as SHA-256 turns any text into a fixed-size fingerprint, called a digest, and it only works in one direction: from the digest you cannot get the text back. So the broker stores sha256(capability) next to the run's scope, and throws the capability itself away after handing it out. When a request arrives, it hashes the token it was shown and looks up that digest. If the table leaks, the thief holds a list of digests, and a digest is useless as a pass: the broker would hash it again and find nothing.

You may have learned that passwords need slow hashes such as bcrypt. That is because people choose guessable passwords, so an attacker can hash a dictionary of common ones and compare. A 256-bit random token is not in any dictionary, so one fast SHA-256 is enough here.
read.see:
$ npx tsx try.ts
capability: 64 characters, starts fc294502
stored digest: 20a2b141a7b5f9bf …
right one: true
same token in capitals: false
empty: false

p: Comparing two strings with === stops at the first character that differs. So a wrong guess whose first ten characters happen to be right takes a tiny bit longer to reject than a guess that is wrong from the start. Over a network that difference is very small, but an attacker can send millions of guesses and measure, and then find the token one character at a time. This is called a timing attack.

timingSafeEqual from node:crypto always compares every byte, so the time it takes says nothing about how close the guess was. It takes two Buffers and throws a RangeError when their lengths differ, which would itself tell the attacker the length. That is why matches hashes the presented text first: both sides are then 32-byte digests, whatever was sent, so the lengths always match.

code.file: what the three versions of the check do
code.text:
presented === stored                       // leaks timing
timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(presented), stored) // RangeError when the lengths differ
timingSafeEqual(sha256(presented), digest)      // always 32 bytes on both sides

notes.text: Fast, and wrong for secrets: the time depends on how many first characters match.
What matches() does: hash first, then compare in constant time.

read.see:
$ npx tsx -e 'import { timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto"; timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from("abc"), Buffer.from("abcd"))'
RangeError: Input buffers must have the same byte length

deeper.h: Go deeper: signed tokens that need no database
p: The gateway, our only door to Claude, checks a run token on every model call, and a database lookup each time would be slow. So its tokens are signed instead of stored. The token carries readable claims (agent, Jira key, run, expiry) plus an HMAC: a hash of the claims mixed with a secret key that only our services hold. To check a token, the gateway computes the HMAC of the claims again with createHmac and compares the two with timingSafeEqual. Change one letter of a claim and the signatures no longer match.
The claims are only encoded with base64url, not encrypted, so anyone holding the token can read them. A claim may say which run this is, but it must never contain a secret.

A secret in a log is a secret for everyone who can read the logs, for as long as the logs are kept. So a token, key or capability never goes into a log line, an error message, a URL, or a test snapshot. The tricky part is that you rarely print a secret on purpose. It arrives inside something else: the headers you log while debugging, or the message of a failed git push, which contains the remote URL, which contains the token.

That is why Byte's broker, the one ours starts from, has a secret guard: before any text leaves the broker, it checks that the text contains none of the secrets the broker knows, and refuses to send it if it does. The guard does not trust every later pull request to be careful; it catches the mistake in code.

notes.text: A named error, so a test can expect exactly this refusal.
Skip empty strings, because every text contains the empty string. The error never repeats the secret.

read.see:
$ npx tsx try-guard.ts
pushed nova/RH-1234
Error: refused: output contains a secret

lab.title: A capability that is random, hashed, compared safely and never printed
lab.goal: Make a capability, store only its digest, check it in constant time, stop it from leaking through an error message, and protect a small server with it.

guess.q: The broker stores only sha256(capability) for each run. Someone steals a copy of that table and sends one of the digests to the broker as a Bearer token. What happens?

options.text: It works: the digest is the stored value, so it matches.
options.why: The broker never compares what it gets with the stored value directly. It hashes what it gets first, and the hash of a digest is a different digest.

options.text: It fails: the broker hashes the token it is shown, and sha256(digest) is not in the table.
options.why: That is the point of storing hashes. Only the original capability hashes to the stored digest, and a hash cannot be turned back into it.

options.text: It works for an hour, until the broker notices the leak.
options.why: Nothing needs to be noticed. A digest was never a valid pass, from the first second.

follow.say: Make the project. Only tsx and the Node types are needed, because node:crypto is built in.
follow.do: mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/p1-4 && cd ~/academy-labs/p1-4 && npm init -y > /dev/null && npm pkg set type=module && npm install -D --save-exact tsx@4.20.3 @types/node@24.12.2 > /dev/null && echo ready

follow.say: Write capability.ts from the first section and a small script that tries it.
follow.see:
capability: 64 characters, starts fc294502
stored digest: 20a2b141a7b5f9bf …
right one: true
same token in capitals: false
empty: false
(your hex is different every run)

follow.say: See why matches() hashes before it compares: timingSafeEqual refuses buffers of different lengths.
follow.do: npx tsx -e 'import { timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto"; timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from("abc"), Buffer.from("abcd"))' 2>&1 | grep RangeError
follow.see: RangeError: Input buffers must have the same byte length

follow.say: Now the leak that nobody writes on purpose: a git error that contains the remote URL, which contains the token. Write the guard and try it.
follow.see:
pushed nova/RH-1234
Error: refused: output contains a secret

lab.build: Protect a server with a capability, like the broker. Write server.ts: it makes a capability with newCapability(), prints it once, and starts a node:http server on port 8080. GET /health answers ok without any token, because Kubernetes calls it. Every other request needs the header Authorization: Bearer <capability>, checked with matches(); anything else gets 401 before any work is done. Start it with npx tsx server.ts in one terminal, and in the other try no header, a wrong token and the right one (copy it from the first terminal into CAP=...).
checks: try.ts printed a 64-character capability, true for the right one and false for the capitals and the empty string.
timingSafeEqual on abc and abcd threw RangeError: Input buffers must have the same byte length.
try-guard.ts printed the safe line and refused the git error.
curl localhost:8080/v1/x without a header and with Bearer guess both get unauthorized [401].
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $CAP" localhost:8080/v1/x gets [200], and /health gets ok without a header.
lab.fix: While chasing a 401, a teammate added console.error("401 for", req.headers.authorization) to the server. It looks harmless, because "it only logs failures". But a failure is often a real capability sent to the wrong service, or one that expired a minute ago, and now it sits in the log system. Add the line, send one request with the right token to the wrong path and one with a typo in the token, and read your terminal. Then remove the line and log only what a person needs: the route and the status.
explain: Why can a leaked table of sha256 digests not be used to call the broker?
Why is presented === stored a problem for a secret, and why does matches() hash before calling timingSafeEqual?
Name two ways a secret can reach a log without anyone printing it on purpose.
lab.done: The server answers 401 without the capability and 200 with it, and nothing you wrote prints a capability except the one line that shows it once.

check.q: Why is one plain SHA-256 enough to store a capability, when passwords need slow hashes like bcrypt?

options.text: Because SHA-256 is newer and stronger than bcrypt
options.why: bcrypt is slow on purpose, which is its strength for passwords. The difference is in what is being hashed, not which function is better.

options.text: Because a 256-bit random token is not in any list of likely guesses, so there is nothing to try against the digest
options.why: Slow hashes protect weak, human-chosen secrets from dictionary guessing. A random 32-byte token has no dictionary.

options.text: Because the capability expires, so it does not matter if someone recovers it
options.why: Expiry helps, but a run can last hours. We store only the digest so that a leaked table is useless from the first second.

check.q: A teammate writes if (presented === stored) for the capability check. What is the risk?

options.text: === may say true for two different strings
options.why: === is exact. The problem is not the answer but how long it takes to give it.
It is usually faster, and that is part of the problem: it stops early.

options.text: It stops at the first wrong character, so the time it takes tells an attacker how much of a guess was right
options.why: That is a timing attack. timingSafeEqual compares every byte every time, so the time says nothing.

check.q: A git push through the broker fails, and the error message from git contains the remote URL https://x-access-token:<token>@github.com/RhinoHealth/fcp.git. What should reach the caller?

options.text: A message without the token, because the secret guard refuses any text that contains a known secret
options.why: Secrets usually leak inside other text, such as an error message. Checking every outgoing text against the known secrets catches that in code.

options.text: The full git message, because the caller needs it to debug the push
options.why: The caller is Nova, which reads text anyone can write. Handing it the GitHub token undoes the whole point of the broker.

options.text: The message with the token in it, but only in the server's own log
options.why: A log is read by many people and kept for a long time. A secret in a log is a leaked secret.

p: When a run starts, the orchestrator asks the broker to open the run's scope (one repo, one branch, one Jira issue, one Slack thread), and the broker answers with a capability made by randomBytes(32). It stores only sha256(capability) with the scope in Postgres, looks every request up by that digest, and refuses an expired scope with 401. The orchestrator also mints the gateway run token, which is HMAC-signed with a key kept in Vault, and writes both passes to the VM with file mode 0600. Both die with the run.

The broker keeps Byte's secret guard, which refuses to return any text that contains the token or the capability, and its tests check that no token appears in any log. The gateway logs only the method, path, status and time of each call.

tickets.why: The broker makes capabilities with randomBytes(32), stores only sha256 digests, compares in constant time and keeps the secret guard.
The gateway's run tokens are HMAC-signed and checked with timingSafeEqual, and its access log holds no content.
The claim step mints both passes for each run and writes them to the VM with mode 0600.

words.plain: A random string that grants one narrow scope to whoever presents it, until it expires.
Node's source of secure random bytes from the operating system. Never use Math.random for secrets.
The fixed-size output of a hash function such as SHA-256. It cannot be turned back into the input.
Finding a secret by measuring how long wrong guesses take to be rejected.
Compares two equal-length Buffers byte by byte in the same time, whatever they contain.
A check that refuses to send or log any text that contains a known secret.

review.q: From memory: the four habits for a capability, from making it to checking it.
review.a: Make it with randomBytes(32), hand it out once and store only sha256 of it, check by hashing what was presented and comparing digests with timingSafeEqual, and never put it in a log, error, URL or snapshot (a guard catches the accidents).

review.q: A teammate wants to put the run token in the URL, /v1/messages?token=..., because it is easier to test with a browser. What do you answer?
review.a: URLs are written to access logs, proxy logs and browser history, so the token would leak. Tokens go in the Authorization header, and the logs hold only the method, path and status.

remember: Make secrets with randomBytes, keep only their hash, compare digests with timingSafeEqual, and never let one reach a log.
